title: An analysis of the guaranteed withdrawal benefits for life option
contribution: Values the guaranteed withdrawal benefits for life (GWB) option in variable annuities: first in closed form under Black-Scholes with exponential retirement lifespans, then under three calibrated asset models. Finds insufficient price discrimination (adverse selection) and large model risk.
problem_entry: AP (finance and insurance): a fast-growing retirement product, GWB for life, 'is yet to be analyzed in detail in the literature'. Earlier GMWB studies ignore the ratchet step-up and rest on Black-Scholes (pp. 1-4). The aim is to value it and size its risk factors for insurers, investors and regulators (p. 1; p. 4).
key_idea: A model ladder: a continuous-time Black-Scholes toy with an analytical value (pp. 8-14), then the realistic product repriced under BSM, SILN (two-factor Vasicek rates) and SISV (adding Heston volatility), all tuned to the same yield curve and implied volatility. The spread across models is reported as 'model risk' (pp. 4-5, 18-22). Investors are assumed to withdraw exactly the guarantee (pp. 6-7); nothing is optimized.
assumptions: Ratchet benefit base, W = 3, A_R = 65, q = 6%, fee 0.65% charged separately from the account (pp. 5-6, 15). Mortality independent of markets and not priced (p. 7). Section 3 assumes continuous step-ups and a constant death intensity (p. 8). PBGC 2008 mortality table (p. 15); sigma_e = 20%, sigma_b = 2%, r = 3.5% (p. 16); no jumps (p. 19); Shiller S&P data 1871-2007 for a backtest (pp. 7-8).
proof_devices: Degree-one homogeneity in (benefit base, account) reduces the state to x = C/B (Proposition 1, pp. 9-10)
Memorylessness after retirement makes values time-independent (Proposition 2, p. 10)
ODE with a smooth-pasting boundary condition shown by a rough discrete-step argument, solved by Whittaker functions (Lemma 1, pp. 10-12)
Joint law of the running maximum and the account via the reflection principle and a change of measure; integrals evaluated numerically (pp. 13-14)
Backward recursion on a 301-point grid with linear interpolation for BSM; Monte Carlo with 10,000 paths for SILN and SISV (pp. 20, 30, 32, 34)
experiments: Net value and break-even fee by cohort age (50-70) and equity exposure (20-80%) (Fig. 1, p. 16; Tables 2-3, pp. 23, 25). Meta-portfolio break-even 0.47% / 0.55% / 0.58% and net value 3.75% / 2.11% / 1.40% of sales under BSM / SILN / SISV (p. 24). Longevity shifted by one year either way (Tables 1, 4, pp. 18, 26). No Monte Carlo errors reported in the parts read.
positioning: Extends GMWB analyses that ignore the ratchet and rest on Black-Scholes (pp. 3-4). Imports rate-risk and systemic-mortality arguments from the annuity literature (pp. 4-5). Questions a jump result for confounding jumps with higher effective volatility (p. 19, fn. 10).
writing: Findings itemized up front in the introduction (pp. 4-5) and repeated as five numbered conclusions addressed to insurers, investors and regulators (pp. 25-26).
limits_future: The Section 3 model 'cannot be used as an absolute valuation tool' (p. 4). No jumps (p. 19); Gaussian rates can turn negative (p. 21); the 65 bp adequacy rests on the assumed investor mix (p. 25). The paper recommends a standardized regulatory pricing model (p. 26); no future research is stated.

method_links.note: Judges the owner's current rule, a single fee of about 50-90 bp for all cohorts and asset mixes, by the insurer's own metrics (net value, break-even fee, liabilities), and recommends pricing by age and investment style. But no decision is optimized, there is no partner or field data, and the recommendation is qualitative.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: model ladder with matched calibration; cross-model spread reported as model risk
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A closed-form toy for intuition, then BSM, SILN and SISV tuned to the same yield curve and one-year ATM implied volatility. The valuation spread (more than 2% of sales) is reported as model risk.

transferable: Look for degree-one homogeneity in the state of a path-dependent valuation to remove a dimension, and for memorylessness to remove time (pp. 9-10).
Calibrate competing models to the same observables (yield curve, ATM implied volatility), so that differences measure structure, not inputs (pp. 5, 21-22).
Backtest the contract on long public data over several windows and show where the conclusion flips (1950-1972 against 1871-1972) (pp. 7-8).
Charge fees outside the account so that break-even fees need no fixed-point solve, and argue that the approximation is small (p. 6, fn. 6).

quotes.text: Our analysis reveals that 1) GWB has insufficient price discrimination and is susceptible to adverse selection and 2) valuations can vary substantially depending on which class of models is used.
We start with a simple model to build intuition and then incrementally refine it to make it more realistic.

title: Robust chirped mirrors
contribution: Applies robust local search to a 208-layer double-chirped mirror pair, searching worst-case thickness errors over a minimum-coherence (Fourier-phase) part of the error shell and moving by SOCP directions. The robust design keeps a high manufacturing yield even beyond the assumed error size.
problem_entry: RO + HS, AP (optics): nominal mirror designs with more than 200 layers fail under nanometre manufacturing errors (p. 1). Prior tolerance methods are first-order or Monte Carlo averages, and convex RO is limited to convex problems (pp. 1-2). Minimize the worst-case merit over a Euclidean ball of layer errors (eqs. (2)-(4), p. 3).
key_idea: Search worst cases on the shell, restricted to minimum-coherence errors (uniform Fourier amplitudes, free phases, no zero-frequency term). This removes systematic shifts and halves the dimension to an unconstrained search (pp. 3-4). An SOCP direction at maximal angle to all worst errors gives the move; its infeasibility signals a robust local minimum (eq. (9), Algorithm 1, p. 4).
assumptions: 208 layers of SiO2/Ta2O5 and 156 wavelengths (650-1200 nm); merit = fourth-power reflectivity error + weighted squared group-delay error (pp. 2-3). Errors independent, additive and normal with sigma = 0.5 nm; systematic errors excluded; Gamma = 0.0075 um for 95% coverage (p. 3). The reduced set is justified empirically: its CDF is within 4% of the full set's (p. 4).
proof_devices: Worst cases on the shell of the ball (cited from the companion paper), used to restrict the inner search (p. 3)
Parseval's theorem keeps Fourier-parametrized errors on the shell; dimension reduced to floor(N/2) (eqs. (6)-(7), p. 4)
SOCP maximizing the angle between the step and all known worst errors, with beta <= -epsilon and a heuristic epsilon (eq. (9), p. 4)
No theorem; the claim that robustness is 'guaranteed to be equal or better' than nominal is stated without proof (p. 2)
experiments: One instance started from the nominal optimum. Worst-case and nominal cost by iteration (Fig. 2, p. 5); worst case as the error ball grows beyond Gamma (Fig. 5, p. 6); Monte Carlo mean and 95th percentile over 10^6 sampled designs per error size (Fig. 6, p. 6). The nominal design is the only baseline; no run times beyond 'on the order of a million' merit evaluations (p. 2).
positioning: Credits Yakovlev-Tempea with showing that design-level robustness can be greatly improved, and differs by probing the exact merit function over a bounded set instead of a Monte Carlo average (pp. 1-2). Cites convex RO (Ben-Tal-Nemirovski, Bertsimas-Sim) as limited to convex problems (p. 2).
writing: Physics-journal style. Claims are hedged ('arguably more robust', p. 2); 'price of robustness' is borrowed as a named term (p. 5).
limits_future: Robust local minimum only (p. 5); fixed layer count (p. 7); Gamma may misstate the true errors (pp. 5-6). Future: use the robust cost inside needle optimization, which changes layer counts (p. 7).

method_links.note: Contradicts the stop rule, not the method's scope: the class is left on purpose for a nonconvex, simulation-given problem, and no solve time is reported; tractability is argued by dimension reduction instead.

The 'price of robustness' is named and shown as the rise in nominal cost and ripple, and performance is plotted against error size. But Gamma is fixed from error statistics, with no curve over a knob and no solution-independent bound.
The nominal optimum is both the warm start and the incumbent beaten; there is no certificate, only SOCP infeasibility with a heuristic epsilon.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: robust local search family: robustify the search, not the model, when no class can be kept
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Neighbourhood ascents on the error shell plus an SOCP step away from worst neighbours, applied to a 208-layer simulator-defined design; the same family appears in S116 and S141.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: stress-test the robust design beyond the set it was built for
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Worst case as the error ball grows beyond the design Gamma, and Monte Carlo yield at error sizes beyond the assumed sigma; also S053, S064, S116.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: cut the uncertainty set to the errors design can fix, and check the cut by Monte Carlo
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Correlated systematic shifts (zero-frequency component) are excluded as unfixable by design and statistically rare; the reduced set's CDF stays within 4% of the full set's.

transferable: Remove from the uncertainty set what design cannot fix (systematic shifts) and what is statistically negligible; check by Monte Carlo that the reduced set gives almost the same cost distribution (pp. 3-4).
Parametrize an error shell by Fourier phases with fixed, equal amplitudes: Parseval keeps the norm, and the worst-case search becomes unconstrained and half the dimension (eqs. (6)-(7), p. 4).
Find a robust descent direction with an SOCP that maximizes the angle to all known worst errors, and use its infeasibility as the stopping test (eq. (9), p. 4).
Report a robust design beyond its tolerance: the worst case as the error ball grows, and the Monte Carlo mean and 95th percentile against error size (Figs. 5-6, p. 6).
coauthors: Omid Nohadani (corresponding), Jonathan R. Birge, Franz X. Kärtner

quotes.text: Optimized chirped mirrors may perform suboptimally, or completely fail to satisfy specifications, when manufacturing errors are encountered.
The unavoidable “price of robustness” through a decrease of the nominal performance of the robust solution is apparent, with increased ripple in the group delay and reflectivity.

title: Approximating integrals of multivariate exponentials: A moment approach
contribution: Brackets integrals of polynomial times exp(polynomial) over compact sets by minimum and maximum SDP moment relaxations built from integration-by-parts relations. Proves that both bounds converge monotonically, and tests order-statistic probabilities.
problem_entry: CP: multivariate integrals (e.g. normal probabilities over compact sets) are computed by Monte Carlo or cubature. Cubature is limited mostly to boxes and simplices, and Genz covers rectangular bivariate and trivariate normals (p. 1). Bound the integral of g e^h over sets given by nested polynomial bounds (eqs. (1)-(2), pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Write the integral as a linear functional of the moments of e^h dx. Integration by parts gives linear equations among these moments and those of boundary measures (eqs. (7)-(9), p. 2). Add PSD moment and localizing matrices, and minimize and maximize the functional: a hierarchy of SDPs that brackets the integral (eq. (14), p. 3).
assumptions: Polynomial g and h; exposition for two variables on a box 'for clarity', with the general case in an ORC technical report (pp. 2, 5). Test cases: Gumbel's bivariate exponential (theta = 0.5) and normals with random mean and factor in [-1, 1] (p. 5); no real data.
proof_devices: Uniqueness: measures satisfying the integration-by-parts relations equal the true measures, via density of polynomials in C^1 and a signed-measure argument (Lemmas 1-2, pp. 3-4)
Convergence: bounded moments, a diagonal subsequence and Putinar's theorem give lower bounds rising and upper bounds falling to the integral (Theorem 1, pp. 4-5)
No rate of convergence is given (pp. 4-5)
experiments: Matlab and SeDuMi on a 2.4 GHz Pentium IV. Gumbel half-gap from 6.5e-3 (r = 2) to 2.9e-9 (r = 5) in 0.38-6.23 s (Table 1, p. 5). 100 random bivariate normals reach 4 digits at average r = 3.64 in about 1 s; trivariate normals take about 250 s (r = 4) and 4000 s (r = 5), 'not competitive' with Genz (p. 5).
positioning: Against Monte Carlo, cubature (de la Harpe-Pache) and Genz's specialized algorithms (p. 1); built on Lasserre's and Laurent's moment-matrix machinery and Putinar's theorem (pp. 3-4).
writing: A numbered list of contributions mapped to sections (p. 1); the general case deferred to a report (p. 2); a plain admission of where the method loses (p. 5).
limits_future: Trivariate run times are large and the method is not competitive with Genz (p. 5). Future: rational integrands, and using the linear relations to eliminate moment variables and shrink the SDPs (p. 5).

method_links.note: A quantity owned by numerical analysis and statistics is written as two SDPs (conic class) whose optimal values bracket it, and the boundary is printed: trivariate cost, and the loss to the specialized code.
No MIO and no warm start, but every answer carries a certificate (the upper-lower half-gap). The incumbent (Genz) is dueled and the loss conceded, while the paper names the cases only it covers.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: two-sided certified bounds from one relaxation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Minimize and maximize the same linear functional over a moment relaxation whose feasible set shrinks to the true measure; the half-gap is the reported error.

transferable: Treat an integral of g e^h as a linear function of moments: generate linear moment equations by integration by parts, add PSD moment and localizing constraints, and solve min and max SDPs for a certified interval (pp. 2-3).
Prove convergence of such a hierarchy by showing that the equations determine the measure uniquely, then use bounded moments, a diagonal subsequence and Putinar (pp. 3-5).
Report the half-gap and the run time at each relaxation order, and stop at a stated tolerance (p. 5).
Name the specialized competitor, concede where you lose, and say what you cover that it does not (p. 5).

quotes.text: We propose a method to calculate lower and upper bounds of some exponential multivariate integrals using moment relaxations and show that they asymptotically converge to the value of the integrals when the moment degree increases.
Clearly, in comparing with results obtained with algorithms specially designed for rectangular normal probabilities by Genz [4], our method for trivariate normal distributions is not competitive.

title: Models for minimax stochastic linear optimization problems with risk aversion
contribution: Reformulates two-stage minimax stochastic LPs with a piecewise-linear risk-averse disutility over mean-covariance ambiguity sets as one polynomial-sized SDP (objective uncertainty). Proves NP-hardness under right-hand-side uncertainty, with a solvable special case, and builds worst-case distributions that serve as stress tests.
problem_entry: RO (distributionally robust) + CP, with LO recourse: distributions are rarely known precisely (p. 1). Minimax stochastic programming (Zackova, Dupacova) and Delage-Ye's ellipsoid-method result are the starting points (pp. 1-2). Minimize the first-stage cost plus the worst expected disutility of the recourse cost over distributions with a given mean and second-moment matrix (problem (2), pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Dualize the inner moment problem (Isii), show the matrix multiplier PSD, swap inf and max (Sion), and write one LMI per disutility piece: one SDP (Theorem 2.1, pp. 4-5). The dual gives conditional moments, hence extremal distributions, and the Jensen bound when risk-neutral (Theorem 2.2, pp. 6-8). The right-hand-side case is NP-hard, and an SDP when the dual extreme points are known (Theorems 3.1-3.2, pp. 9-10).
assumptions: Ambiguity set: all distributions on R^p with a known mean and second-moment matrix (eq. (4), p. 3). Bounded first-stage polytope, complete fixed recourse, dual feasibility, positive definite covariance (Assumptions 1-4, p. 3). Known dual extreme points for the right-hand-side SDP (Assumption 5, p. 10). Synthetic instances only (pp. 14, 19).
proof_devices: Moment-problem duality (Isii); PSD of the multiplier by scaling along the most negative eigenvector; Sion's minimax theorem; one LMI per piece (Theorem 2.1, pp. 4-5)
Feasible dual point built from any distribution through conditional moments (Lemma 2.1, p. 6); limiting extremal distributions from Bernoulli mixtures as epsilon -> 0 (Theorem 2.2, pp. 7-8)
NP-hardness via the separation problem, by reduction from 2-norm maximization over a polytope (Mangasarian-Shiau), using the equivalence of separation and optimization (Theorem 3.1, pp. 9-10)
Delayed constraint generation over dual extreme points with a biconvex separation step (p. 12)
experiments: Production-transportation (5 facilities, 20 customers) and single-facility minimax distance (20 customers); minimax SDP (Matlab, SeDuMi, YALMIP) against a data-driven LP on 10,000 normal samples (CPLEX 9.1) (pp. 13-14, 19). Costs under each solution's extremal distribution and under contamination (1 - lambda) P_d + lambda P_worst(x_d): minimax wins on mean cost beyond lambda = 0.75 / 0.5 and on dispersion for nearly all lambda (pp. 15-22). No run times reported.
positioning: Minimax stochastic programming from Zackova and Dupacova; Delage-Ye compared head-on and credited with the broader class (pp. 1-2, 5). Risk measures from Ahmed, Eichorn-Romisch and Ben-Tal-Teboulle (p. 2). Dupacova's contamination test adopted and given a choice of contaminating distribution (pp. 15-16).
writing: Contributions as a numbered list keyed to sections (p. 3); theorem-proof style; no conclusion section, the paper ends with Section 4.2 (p. 22).
limits_future: The general right-hand-side case is NP-hard; the dual extreme points can be very many; separation is biconvex (p. 12). No future work is stated.

method_links.note: A problem owned by stochastic programming is written as one polynomial-sized SDP, its dual read as the worst-case distribution, and the boundary printed as NP-hardness for right-hand-side uncertainty.
No knob: the price of protection is read along a contamination axis, with the minimax plan costing more under the data distribution and winning past a crossover in lambda.
The standard practice, a sample-based solution, is the baseline, and decisions are scored by realized cost under contamination; but the data are synthetic and there is no owner.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: worst-case distribution from the dual as a stress test for any candidate solution
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Solve the data-driven model, compute its own extremal distribution from the SDP dual, and test both solutions on the mixture (1 - lambda) P_d + lambda P_worst.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: stress-test the robust solution beyond the set it was built for
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Contamination sweep from lambda = 0 to 1, reporting mean, standard deviation and quadratic semideviation; also S278, S064, S116.

transferable: For a sup of an expectation over a mean-covariance class: dualize to a semi-infinite constraint, prove the multiplier PSD by scaling along its most negative eigenvector, swap min and max by Sion, and write one LMI per piece (pp. 4-5).
Read the dual SDP variables as scaled conditional moments and build the extremal distribution from them (pp. 5-8).

Stress test: compute the data-driven solution's own worst-case distribution, mix it in with weight lambda from 0 to 1, and compare solutions by mean, standard deviation and upper semideviation (pp. 16-17).
Prove NP-hardness of a robust or minimax model through its separation problem and the equivalence of separation and optimization (pp. 9-10).
coauthors: Xuan Vinh Doan, Karthik Natarajan, Chung-Piaw Teo

quotes.text: The minimax solutions thus guarantee to hedge against these worst possible distributions and provide a natural distribution to stress test stochastic optimization problems under distributional ambiguity.
This suggests that if there is significant uncertainty in the knowledge of the exact distribution, the minimax solution would be a better choice.

title: A soft robust model for optimization under ambiguity
contribution: Introduces soft robustness, guarantees that weaken across a nested family of ambiguity sets, and shows it is equivalent to convex-risk-measure constraints. Solves it by a few standard robust problems, gives downside probability bounds under ambiguity, and tests it on a bond portfolio and on 25 years of asset-allocation data.
problem_entry: RO (ambiguity), AP (finance): how should a set of distributions be obtained, and why treat all distributions inside it equally while ignoring those outside (p. 1)? Standard robustness can relax only by shrinking the set (p. 3). Maximize the expected payoff subject to E_Q f(x) >= -epsilon for all Q in Q(epsilon), for all epsilon >= 0 (eq. (4), p. 3).
key_idea: Soft robustness, a nested convex family with linearly relaxing guarantees, is equivalent to a normalized convex-risk-measure constraint, so feasibility is jointly convex (Theorem 2.1, pp. 4-5). It is solvable by bisection over standard robust problems (Proposition 2.1, p. 7). Downside bounds under ambiguity follow from one-dimensional convex problems (Theorem 3.1, pp. 10-11).
assumptions: Payoff concave in x and bounded; X closed and convex (p. 3); phi-divergence families, with relative entropy, Hellinger, OCE and CVaR as cases (pp. 6-7). Bonds: 49 independent defaults with probabilities in [0.001, 0.05], 20% leverage cap (pp. 11-12). Assets: 11 classes, monthly returns 1981-2006, 36-month window, yearly rebalancing, no transaction costs (p. 14; endnote 7, p. 15). Entropic parameter 50 because convenient (endnote 6, p. 15).
proof_devices: Follmer-Schied dual representation of convex risk measures; joint convexity in (mu, x) of the scaled risk measure (Theorem 2.1, pp. 4-5)
Concavity of the value function in the robustness level, justifying bisection over standard robust problems (Proposition 2.1, p. 7; proof in the appendix, not in the file)
Post-solution conservatism comparison: standard robust optima are soft robust up to a level computed from the dual multiplier (Proposition 2.2, p. 8)
Tail bounds from OCEs, tightened with the support and inflated over a divergence ball (Lemma 3.1, p. 9; Theorem 3.1, pp. 10-11)
experiments: Bonds: ROME in MATLAB, about 30 s per problem. At rho = 1.1 standard robust holds 80%+ in the riskless asset for +0.05% expected return, while soft robust earns about 1.2% more expected return and over 14% more maximum return (pp. 12-13). Assets: against CVaR, standard and comprehensive robust over 25 years out of sample, soft robust beat standard robust in every case (+0.38% on average) at some extra downside, and beat CVaR on realized risk for alpha = 0.3-0.8 (p. 14).
positioning: Builds on the RO founders and on the economics of ambiguity (Ellsberg, Gilboa-Schmeidler, Hansen-Sargent, Maccheroni et al.), not on preferences (pp. 1-2). Distinguishes Fischetti-Monaci light robustness (optimality enforced, feasibility an output) from soft robustness (feasibility levels enforced, optimality an output) (p. 2).
writing: Opens with two critiques posed as questions (p. 1); each theorem followed by an interpretation (pp. 5, 7-8); empirical claims hedged ('seemingly favorable', p. 1).
limits_future: No explicit optimality bound from Proposition 2.2 (p. 8); the OCE bound is 'often loose' (p. 10); in-sample CVaR constraints generally fail out of sample (p. 14); no transaction costs (p. 15). Future: explain the out-of-sample benefit, perhaps with statistical learning theory (p. 14).

method_links.note: The property is protection against ambiguity, with one interpretable knob (error factor rho on default probabilities), solution-independent downside bounds (Theorem 3.1) and a priced table with its bad case (standard robustness highly conservative even at small rho). The entropic parameter is fixed for convenience (endnote 6), supporting the skill's correction that knobs get fixed arbitrarily.
Soft robustness keeps convexity and costs only a few standard robust solves.
A 25-year rolling out-of-sample test against the practitioners' benchmark (CVaR), with decision metrics (realized CVaR, loss probabilities); no owner or partner.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: graded guarantees over nested uncertainty sets (soft robustness) as the remedy for over-conservatism
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Guarantees relax linearly across a nested family of ambiguity sets; comprehensive robustness (Example 2.3) adds a hard core set; light robustness is contrasted.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: stress-test the robust solution beyond the set it was built for
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Out-of-sample, 25-year rolling test with realized CVaR and loss probabilities; also S278, S053, S116.

transferable: Replace a single uncertainty set by a nested family whose guarantee relaxes linearly with the set's size; check the equivalence with a convex risk measure, so that the constraint stays convex (pp. 3-5).
When a constraint must hold at a continuum of levels, prove the value function concave in the level and bisect, solving one standard robust problem per step (p. 7).
Tighten risk-measure tail bounds with the support (a payoff upper bound), then inflate them for ambiguity through a one-dimensional convex problem over a divergence ball (pp. 9-11).
Calibrate the robust parameter to the benchmark: take the smallest level whose robust constraint is no weaker than the CVaR constraint (p. 13).

quotes.text: relaxing standard robustness with soft robustness yields a seemingly favorable risk-return trade-off: each case results in a higher out-of-sample expected return for a relatively minor degradation of out-of-sample downside performance.
We note that Proposition 2.2 provides a generic result relating the standard robust and soft robust approaches, but it does not provide any explicit bounds on the difference in optimality.

title: Nonconvex robust optimization for problems with constraints
contribution: Extends robust local search to nonconvex problems with constraints and parameter uncertainty, using feasibility and cost moves by SOCP directions and closed forms for convex constraints. Applies it to a polynomial example and to an 85-variable IMRT beam-angle and intensity problem.
problem_entry: RO + HS, AP (health care, IMRT): RO had focused on convex, explicitly structured problems, and the authors' earlier method was unconstrained (p. 1). Minimize the worst-case cost over a Euclidean error ball subject to each constraint's worst case <= 0 (problem (10), p. 3); parameters are folded into the decision vector (eq. (22), p. 6).
key_idea: Neighbourhood gradient ascents find high-cost and infeasible neighbours. A feasibility SOCP moves away from infeasible neighbours while the design is not robust; a cost SOCP moves away from high-cost neighbours and from infeasible designs just beyond the neighbourhood once it is. The search stops at a robust local minimum (Definition 1, Algorithm 2, pp. 3-5). Convex constraints get closed-form inner maxima, and linear ones exact robust counterparts (Table 1, p. 5).
assumptions: Implementation errors in a 2-norm ball; cost, constraints and gradients from a simulator (pp. 1-2). Application I: 2-D polynomial with two nonconvex constraints, Gamma = 0.5 (pp. 7-8). Application II: 1,192 voxels, 85 variables (80 beamlets + 5 angles), CERR doses at 2-degree steps with interpolation, normal errors; the case downsized for numerical reasons, with second-order terms dropped (pp. 10-11).
proof_devices: SOCP angle-maximization for feasibility and cost directions (eqs. (7), (14), (15), pp. 2-4)
Termination by Definition 1: feasible under perturbation, no improving direction (p. 4)
Closed-form inner maxima for convex constraints: LP for linear, single trust-region SDP for quadratic, one ascent for concave; exact counterpart a'x + Gamma ||a|| + b <= 0 (Table 1, p. 5)
Parameter uncertainty by stacking parameters into the decision vector with zero step (pp. 6-7); no convergence theorem
experiments: Application I: two starts reach two robust local minima, worst-case cost cut by more than 70%, under 10 min on a 3.4 GHz Xeon; 96 s instead of 3,600 s with explicit linear counterparts (pp. 8-9, 15). Application II: Gamma swept in 0.001 steps from two starts, designs scored on 10,000 normal scenarios, Pareto frontiers of mean cost against violation probability, about 20 h per search (pp. 12-13). Against convex RO with fixed angles (LPs under 5 s after SOCPs took CPLEX 9.1 hours): convex wins at high violation probability, robust local search below 2% (p. 14).
positioning: Builds on their unconstrained robust local search (S090) and convex RO (p. 1). Judges polynomial SDP relaxations (Henrion-Lasserre, Kojima) not yet practical (p. 8). Claims joint robustness over beam angles and intensities 'for the first time', where Chan-Bortfeld-Tsitsiklis fixed the angles (p. 10).
writing: An intuition-building 2-D application precedes the real one (p. 1); figures carry the algorithm's geometry (Figs. 1-5, pp. 2-7); the conclusion restates the numbers (p. 15).
limits_future: Local minima only, and several of them (p. 8); worst-case cost estimated by sampling, 'not a good gauge' (p. 13); 20 h runs (p. 13); the clinical case downsized (p. 10). No future work stated.

method_links.note: The class is left on purpose (no practical method even for the 2-D robust polynomial problem), but kept wherever a constraint is convex through exact counterparts, with the gain measured (96 s against 3,600 s).

Gamma is the knob, swept to map the Pareto frontier in a single sweep, which is handed to clinicians to choose a violation probability; but violation probabilities are measured by sampling, with no solution-independent bound.
A duel with the incumbent (convex RO with fixed angles) reports where each method wins (the 2% threshold); there is no certificate.
The model comes from a hospital partner (MGH), and the nominal plan is the baseline, which always violates the constraints under uncertainty; there is no field test.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Gamma-continuation to trace the robustness-cost Pareto frontier
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Increase the uncertainty size in steps of 0.001, warm-starting each robust local search from the last design, from two starts (nominal best, strict interior).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: robust local search family: robustify the search, not the model, when no class can be kept
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Constrained robust local search with feasibility and cost SOCP moves; also S278 and S141.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: stress-test the robust solution beyond the set it was built for
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Every design scored on 10,000 sampled scenarios for mean cost and violation probability; also S278, S053, S064.

transferable: In constrained robust local search, first restore feasibility under perturbation and ignore cost; then cut the worst-case cost while avoiding infeasible designs within a radius enlarged to (1 + delta) Gamma (pp. 3-4).
Replace sampled inner maximizations by closed forms wherever a constraint is convex (LP, trust-region SDP, one ascent), and time the gain (pp. 5, 9).
Handle parameter uncertainty in an implementation-error algorithm by stacking parameters into the decision vector with zero steps (pp. 6-7).
Trace the robustness frontier from two different starts (nominal optimum, strict interior) and score all designs on the same sampled scenarios (pp. 12-13).
Build a convex comparator by fixing the nonconvex variables (beam angles) and report the regime where each method wins (p. 14).

quotes.text: The proposed method iteratively moves along descent directions for the robust problem with nonconvex constraints and terminates at a robust local minimum.
The original treatment plan, found using optimization without consideration for uncertainties, proves to always violate the constraints when uncertainties are introduced.

title: On the power of robust solutions in two-stage stochastic and adaptive optimization problems
contribution: Proves that a static robust solution costs at most twice the optimal two-stage stochastic cost (right-hand-side uncertainty, symmetric sets and measures), at most 2 or 4 times the fully adaptive cost, and exactly the adaptive cost for hypercubes. Each bound comes with tight and unbounded-gap examples.
problem_entry: RO + IO: stochastic optimization is 'by and large computationally intractable', robust optimization tractable but possibly conservative, and adaptive optimization hard to approximate (pp. 1-3). How much does one static robust solution lose against the stochastic optimum (stochasticity gap) and the fully adaptive optimum (adaptability gap), for covering-type two-stage mixed-integer problems (pp. 2-5)?
key_idea: A symmetric set in the nonnegative orthant lies below twice its centre (Lemma 2.3, p. 8). Doubling the centre-scenario solution is robust-feasible, and linearity with no second-stage integers bounds robust <= 2 x stochastic (Theorem 2.1, pp. 7-9). The same move gives bounds for positive sets, adaptability gaps <= 2 (right-hand side) and <= 4 (with costs), and a gap of 1 for hypercubes (Theorems 2.7, 4.1, 5.1, 5.3, pp. 14-21).
assumptions: Ax + By >= b with c, d >= 0, nonnegative mixed-integer variables and b >= 0, which excludes packing constraints and maximization (pp. 2-4); no complete recourse needed (p. 3). Symmetric measure, or the weaker E[b] >= b0 (pp. 7-8). The bounds fail with binary variables (pp. 10, 16). No data.
proof_devices: Bounding hypercube and point of symmetry: every point of a symmetric nonnegative set is at most twice the centre (Lemmas 2.2-2.3, p. 8)
Scaling the centre-scenario solution by 2 for robust feasibility, plus linearity of expectation (proof of Theorem 2.1, p. 9)

Tight example: hypercube with uniform b gives gap exactly 2 (Theorem 2.5, p. 12); unbounded examples: simplex set with gap n + 1 (Theorem 2.6, p. 13), cost uncertainty via E[min of n uniforms] = 1/(n + 1) (Theorem 3.1, p. 15)
Worst-corner scenario of a hypercube (min A, B; max b, d) gives an adaptability gap of 1 even with uncertain constraint coefficients (Theorem 5.3, pp. 20-21)
positioning: Robust optimization set between stochastic programming's intractability (Shapiro-Nemirovski) and adaptive optimization's inapproximability (Feige et al.), with affine policies (including his work with Iancu-Parrilo and with Goyal) as the usual compromise (pp. 1-3). Stochastic set-cover approximation models are more restrictive and need complete recourse (pp. 3-4).
writing: Results summarized in two tables with tightness marks (p. 6); positive results called 'surprising' (pp. 5, 18, 21); each bound followed by its tightness or counterexample.
limits_future: Covering structure, nonnegativity, no binaries; the stochasticity gap is unbounded under cost uncertainty (pp. 4, 10, 15). The conclusion claims RO is 'more powerful than believed previously' (p. 21); no future work stated.

method_links.note: The tractable static robust model, 'a single mixed integer optimization problem' independent of the scenarios and of the distribution, stands in for intractable stochastic and adaptive models; the boundary of the claim is mapped by counterexamples.
The price of static robustness is given as solution-independent worst-case ratios with the bad cases printed (nonsymmetric sets, cost uncertainty); there is no knob or curve.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: bracket every approximation bound with a tight example and an unbounded example on the next wider class, in one table
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Tables 1-2 mark tight bounds; Theorems 2.5, 2.6, 3.1, 4.3 and 4.4 give tight and large-gap instances for each relaxation of the assumptions.

transferable: Bound a robust-against-stochastic gap by scaling the centre-scenario solution: if every scenario is at most twice the centre (symmetric nonnegative sets), doubling it is robust-feasible (pp. 8-9).
State the weakest distributional condition the proof uses (E[b] >= b0 instead of symmetry), and say which result needs which (pp. 7-8).
For each bound, give a tight instance and an unbounded instance one assumption away, collected in a table with tightness marks (pp. 6, 12-18).
Extend symmetric-set results to 'positive' sets (inside a symmetric set whose centre lies in the set), which covers budget sets such as k-fault tolerance (pp. 4, 14).

quotes.text: We refer to the ratio of the optimal cost of the robust problem and the optimal cost of the two-stage stochastic problem as the stochasticity gap.

Therefore, the results in this paper show that the robust optimization approach is more powerful than believed previously and provides a tractable and good approximation for both the two-stage stochastic and the two-stage adaptive optimization problem under fairly general assumptions.

title: Robust optimization with simulated annealing
contribution: Proposes robust simulated annealing, a Metropolis search on a soft-max of worst-case neighbour costs, with a claimed global convergence theorem. Demonstrates it on a 2-D polynomial and a 100-dimensional nanophotonic design.
problem_entry: HS + RO, AP (nanophotonics): optimized designs fail under implementation errors (p. 2). Convex RO is 'limited to convex problems', and earlier robust local searches gave only local optima (p. 2). Find the global minimum of g(x) = max over ||dx|| <= Gamma of f(x + dx) with only a black box for f and its derivative (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Bad neighbours are found by gradient ascents. The worst case is smoothed as a log-sum-exp at inverse temperature beta (eq. (3), p. 4). Gaussian trial moves are accepted by Metropolis on Boltzmann weights, with beta grown by Eq. (7) (pp. 4-5). For photonics, adaptive sampling, re-annealing and re-heating are added (pp. 9-10).
assumptions: f unrestricted; 2-norm ball (pp. 2-3). Theorem 1 assumes a bounded set of minima, a global robust optimum, and equal accessibility of all designs as n -> infinity (p. 5). Applications: the S116 polynomial with Gamma = 0.5 (p. 6); 50 cylinders (100 coordinates) with a lab-verified finite-difference model, sigma = 40 um, Gamma = 550 um for 99% coverage (pp. 8-9).
proof_devices: Global convergence (Theorem 1) by citing Geman-Geman's condition that beta grow no faster than ln(n)/beta0, Ingber's bound for the Gaussian generator, and detailed balance (pp. 5-6)
[inferred] As extracted, Eq. (7) makes beta grow exponentially in n, yet the proof states that the first condition is satisfied by Eq. (7); extraction loses symbols, so check the PDF (p. 5)
Convergence rate declared out of scope (p. 6)
experiments: Polynomial: optimum checked by enumerating the worst-case function on a fine mesh, one run shown (pp. 7-8). Photonics: re-annealing against re-annealing plus re-heating (Fig. 4, p. 10); against the earlier ~8% robust-local-search result from the same start (pp. 9-10; Fig. 5 labelled 8% and 40%, p. 11). No RSA wall-clock times, no repeated-run statistics; runs stopped at an empirical threshold (p. 11).
positioning: After convex RO (limited to convex problems) and the authors' own local robust searches (local optima) (p. 2); lineage Kirkpatrick et al., Metropolis, Geman-Geman, Ingber (pp. 3, 5); polynomial SDPs dismissed as 'not widely used in practice' (p. 7).
writing: Opens with famous failures (Tacoma Narrows, p. 2); strong, unhedged claims ('warrants', p. 9; 'any previously available methods', p. 12).
limits_future: Parameters problem-specific and 'cannot be generalized' (p. 10); rate out of scope (p. 6); runs non-deterministic (p. 11). No future work stated.

method_links.note: Claims RSA 'warrants a global robust optimum' for runs stopped at an empirical threshold, on the strength of an asymptotic theorem, with no certificate, gap or equal-time duel. This is against Method 4's rule never to call uncertified results optimal, and against the 1993 review S005's yardsticks (time-asymptotic results 'largely irrelevant'; equal computing time). Evidence for Tensions T1 and T2.
The class is left; the case against convex relaxations is that polynomial SDPs grow with degree and dimension and are not widely used in practice.
'Price of robustness' names the slight rise in nominal cost; there is no knob or curve.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: robust local search family: robustify the search, not the model, when no class can be kept
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Here a global stochastic version: annealing on a log-sum-exp of bad-neighbour costs; also S278 and S116.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: asymptotic convergence theorem offered as a global-optimality claim for an empirically stopped heuristic (anti-pattern evidence for T1/T2)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 1 (asymptotic) plus 'warrants a global robust optimum', while runs end at an empirical threshold, with no gap or equal-time comparison.

transferable: Smooth a worst case over sampled bad neighbours into a log-sum-exp at the annealing temperature, so that Metropolis compares worst cases at equal beta (pp. 4, 6).
Check a claimed global robust optimum on a low-dimensional instance by enumerating the worst-case function on a fine mesh before going high-dimensional (p. 7).
Size the uncertainty ball from measured error statistics for a stated coverage (sigma = 40 um -> Gamma = 550 um for 99%) (p. 9).

quotes.text: Therefore, applying the proposed RSA to this model warrants a global robust optimum.
We terminated the simulations in Fig. 5 after the number of trials for the same acceptance step exceeded an empirical threshold.
